interest: This file offers a compelling window into the ideological dynamics of Vichy-controlled French North Africa mere months before the Allied landings in Operation Torch. It highlights how collaborationist authorities in Morocco sought to align colonial and French youth with the Axis cause by romanticizing Japanese Imperial ideology, Bushido, and State Shinto as moral alternatives to Western democratic individualism and historic Franco-American friendship. It also documents the active intelligence-gathering and propaganda-monitoring role played by the U.S. Consulate General in Casablanca during a pivotal phase of the Second World War.
overview: This file consists of Despatch No. 692 of August 4, 1942, from H. Earle Russell, American Consul General in Casablanca, Morocco, to the Secretary of State, enclosing an English translation of a Vichy French collaborationist propaganda article from the August 2, 1942 issue of the Moroccan youth periodical Jeunesse. In his despatch, Russell alerts Washington to an expanding media campaign in Morocco that glorifies the Axis powers and Imperial Japan while disparaging the United States and exploiting historic Anglo-French grievances to sway impressionable youth away from traditional Franco-American ties. The enclosed article, authored by Pierre Cordier of the Sécurité Publique in Rabat, presents an idealized portrait of Japan's fusion of church and state under the Emperor, citing the 1890 Imperial Rescript of Emperor Meiji and Inazo Nitobe's writings to promote Japanese martial discipline, collective virtue, and self-sacrificing fatalism as a model for youth.

people.name: Pierre Cordier

subfiles.about: Transmittal of a translation of a collaborationist youth newspaper article along with an assessment of pro-Axis and pro-Japanese propaganda efforts in French Morocco.
subfiles.from: H. Earle Russell, American Consul General, Casablanca
subfiles.summary: American Consul General H. Earle Russell informs the Secretary of State that Moroccan newspapers and periodicals are increasingly glorifying Japan and the Axis powers to diminish American influence. He observes that while older French citizens remain skeptical due to Japan's actions in Indochina, uninformed youth are vulnerable to this propaganda, which exploits historic Anglo-French antagonism while omitting the legacy of Franco-American friendship. As an example, he transmits a translation of an article published in the Moroccan youth weekly "Jeunesse" written by collaborationist Pierre Cordier.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 692 from H. Earle Russell (Casablanca) on Axis and Japanese Propaganda in Moroccan Youth Publications

subfiles.about: English translation of a collaborationist article extolling Japan's theocratic imperial governance, martial culture, and ethos of total self-sacrifice.
subfiles.summary: Pierre Cordier argues that Japan's military victories derive from its unified system of church and state, in which the Emperor serves as both spiritual and temporal leader of an egalitarian, devoted national family. Quoting Emperor Meiji's 1890 Imperial Rescript on Education and citing Inazo Nitobe, the author contrasts Japanese collective virtue, spiritual discipline, and readiness for martyrdom with Western individualism and materialism. The article romanticizes warrior suicides, human torpedoes, and aviators sacrificing their lives, depicting self-immolation for the Emperor as the ultimate expression of honor and duty.
subfiles.title: Translation of Article "Japan Wins Its Battles by Its Established System of Church and State" by Pierre Cordier in "Jeunesse"
